(Angelina Katsanis/AP Photo/Angelina Katsanis)"},{"_id":"3LO5JFVODFAGXISMMVCN5CVWGY","type":"text","content":"In August 2001, I was fresh out of college, living with four roommates in a converted TriBeCa loft that offered a panoramic view of lower Manhattan and the World Trade Center, standing proudly just eight blocks away.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"2CUU7K4BLNF4JMEEE4DXQJ5SKU","type":"text","content":"I found the apartment on Church and Chambers Streets through dumb luck. A friend of my brother’s was moving out and needed someone to take her place to live with four very cool and attractive women who would be moving out just weeks after she did.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"GOMZTWATGZCPNLFTHZNPJWCZRY","type":"text","content":"I had scored a jackpot: the perfect first apartment. I was living in the city where I’d grown up, working as an intern for a production company that paid little and offered no promise of full-time employment. The new roommates who replaced the old ones were a lot like me: 22, starting their adult lives, with no idea about next steps. But we’d forget our anxieties when we’d go up to the building’s roof to drink beer and take in the stillness of the late-night cityscape, hear the occasional passing taxi, and behold those indomitable Twin Towers rising above us, often half-concealed by overcast skies, with only the glints of office lights still visible through the clouds.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"TWSV6XVS75FKDJG5EY6XDQSFHI","type":"text","content":"At 8:46 a.m. on September 11, 2001, I was in the apartment, running late for work, when an airplane flew right above our building, shaking it and everything around us, before crashing into the North Tower. It felt and sounded like a missile hitting its target at full bore. I raced out into the living room. The impact had left a gaping hole in the top of the tower. I watched the fire and smoke billow out of the crater and tried to process what just happened. Maybe a helicopter had lost control? Someone took a fighter jet from the Intrepid on a joyride? I called my boss to tell him that something had flown into the World Trade Center and that I would try to make it in once things settled down.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"2AOYDWCFNFEABFHQXQKH4LVE3M","type":"text","content":"Two of my roommates, Em and Stef, stood now in the living room, too, half-awake and confused. We turned on the TV, looking for updates, then went up to the roof to get a better view. Emergency vehicles of all kinds were racing south against northbound traffic on Church Street. Office workers still carrying their computer bags or briefcases stood uneasily on the sidewalks, watching the scene unfold. I remember looking at the flames and wondering whether firefighters had any chance of putting out a blaze that high up.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"YCQPEIS5RRHXJICEN22XKGJKFE","type":"text","content":"Some construction workers on the roof of an adjacent building waved us over. They pointed to a basketball-sized hole in the roof caused by a chunk of broken concrete. They said it was shrapnel caused by the plane’s impact, sending it flying several blocks over here from the North Tower.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"XXZ5C27HW5CLVJF6H4J4KLGPHY","type":"text","content":"Our cell phones weren’t working but the landline was, so we called our families. My parents, then in Europe, told me to stay in the apartment for as long as I could. I reached my brother, who was studying near Washington Square Park. He was fine.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"N4TEYBQSNJG6XPNMEBSUPOURRY","type":"text","content":"Em, Stef and I reconvened in the living room to watch the news, still clueless as to what had flown into the North Tower, when we heard it—dreadful, shrill, and fast. Then we saw it, a hideous inferno that fanned out in every direction.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"IMWVBURGFJCEJOUWZVGQJZTCOI","type":"text","content":"“They’re doing it again! They’re doing it again!” Stef screamed.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"PZZVWWUKN5GRLCZNNTO4UF3UZE","type":"text","content":"The fireball hung in the air for what felt like minutes, mutating itself from orange to black smoke. On the street below came the sound of screaming and wailing. People were running north on Church. Cops had set up a checkpoint on Chambers. Emergency vehicles kept racing down toward the site.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"JOB46UXHRJH4DGXGXLK6SASWNE","type":"text","content":"We could now smell the acrid smoke, a scent that endured in our living room and walls and clothes for what felt like months afterward. We flipped through news channels and debated what to do. We couldn’t stay here for long. I’d be able to take refuge in my childhood apartment uptown, but Em and Stef were both new to the city from the Bay Area. All they had was a friend from college who lived in Midtown and worked for a finance firm whose offices were located near World Trade.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"IA7BADD4ERHQBNKE53VCJABWEY","type":"text","content":"I was watching a helicopter circling the North Tower when I noticed the top of the South Tower start to buckle. Then it started coming down.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"TYLZ5BXDY5HEBMQT3XSD5S44GQ","type":"text","content":"The three of us ran out of the apartment and into the back stairwell, waiting, it seemed, for our building’s turn to collapse. We stood there for minutes. It was quiet. No screams from outside. I only heard our collective breathing. We went down to the lobby. Outside, the air was thick with ash and soot. Then came a light tapping of long fingernails against the glass of the front doors.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"4MBJ23LKNZHSTA6HDHEICL7X2M","type":"text","content":"It was a woman, middle-aged, dressed in black work clothes. We let her in and with Stef’s water bottle poured water in her hands so she could wash off the soot from outside. She was hyperventilating. She needed to call her family in Long Island. I brought her upstairs to use the landline while Em and Stef brought passersby into the lobby to wash ash out of their eyes. A cop told Em and Stef we had to vacate the building immediately.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"D6NKNISPMZG4TPJAQH2ONJUZTY","type":"text","content":"We packed our backpacks with clothes. We left without bothering to close our living room windows.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"IT43SIYURJFUZE3ZLCQPN2ME34","type":"text","content":"Outside, it was mayhem. Everyone was sprinting, and soon we were, too. Cops yelled at us to keep moving. Someone behind us called out, “package bomb!” and we ran faster. We made it to the Canal Street checkpoint, where I squeezed past a tall man on a bike holding a professional-grade camcorder high up toward the sky, blocking the flow of human traffic. We stopped running at West Houston. I promised to walk Stef and Em to their friend’s place in Hell’s Kitchen. Once they were settled, I would make my own way home.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"ZSDHB2DE3RAFXEGYYLM2JQLZR4","type":"text","content":"When we reached Chelsea, we met two teenagers who had managed to sneak out of their high school, even as the headmaster put everyone on emergency lockdown. They asked us if they could use our cell phones to call their families, but it was no use—no cell service.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"MEDGUZ2A3JHQHI6NQAJL4TX6MU","type":"text","content":"Nearly an hour into our pilgrimage north, we reached Times Square, where the sidewalks were choked with onlookers, their heads craned up at the jumbo screens and the news tickers. We learned that the North Tower had collapsed now, too. Both were gone, in a matter of hours. We kept moving north with everyone else.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"CCQKJFES7ZCJ7CEVLXD3JRTI24","type":"text","content":"We picked up bottles of wine and whiskey for Em and Stef’s friend, and we were relieved to learn from her doorman, when we arrived, that she was expecting us.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"BJ6KQVKYSVGJLPBWQ2YFPJX7ZI","type":"text","content":"Their friend, who I will call Grace, let us in, and we all set to work on the whiskey and sharing our eyewitness accounts. Grace had been at work in her office (not in the World Trade Center, but nearby when the first plane hit. She did not wait for company permission to leave. She grabbed her purse, ran down 20 flights of stairs to the lobby, and entered the nearest sporting goods store. Pointing at a store clerk watching the news on TV, she said, “I’m a size 6 women’s, and I have a credit card. Give me whatever running shoes you have and let me get the hell out of here.”","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"ETGVHE5URJB3PK3G6AXUFEJV3U","type":"text","content":"The whiskey didn’t last long. Grace offered me a sofa to sleep on; I thanked her and declined. Em and Stef were safe, drunk, and sheltered, about as good an outcome as anyone could want on this day.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"2R2M4GI4K5DFZCD42FRFFIO4ZI","type":"text","content":"Walking east through Central Park, I noticed the day’s weather for the first time: a spotless sky, sunny and warm. On the grasses and in the playgrounds families were at play, parents and toddlers seemingly oblivious to the events. There were no iPhones, so news wasn’t as instantaneous. But word must have spread around by then.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"KWARRHLY4ZHHRG5VOF5WGNAIIE","type":"text","content":"I watched a family in Heckscher Playground. A young boy no older than three sat in the sand. His parents stood behind him, hands on hips, smiling. I wanted to approach them and ask if they knew what had just happened. It took only a second to banish the thought. My ears were ringing. My adrenaline was raging. I would look and sound insane. Besides, they needed to take in these last few moments of normalcy before it escaped them for good.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"VOO6FLSOPJGM3D37LB7WTPZT2Q","type":"text","content":"So I continued my walk toward home, where I hoped to find my brother. Soon that family would also leave the idyll of Central Park and journey home through an unfamiliar city.","additional_properties":{}}],"description":{"basic":"A lifelong New Yorker remembers September President JD Vance is promoting a \u003ca href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/05/us/politics/stay-at-home-parents-subsidies.html\"\u003eTrump administration plan\u003c/a\u003e to siphon off federal money that helps working parents afford childcare and use it to subsidize parents who stay at home. The man who ran for office mocking “childless cat ladies” is now trying to stir up a cat fight between working and stay-at-home moms. That’s not remarkable coming from a federal government run by social media trolls. But the main effect of the actual policy Vance is promoting will be to make the lives of already stressed working class families, especially in Wisconsin, even harder, more expensive and noticeably worse than before.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"EVHUYM26NJHUJNSD2YFXU2ZA6M","type":"text","content":"Childcare funding has been in crisis in Wisconsin ever since the pandemic relief money that briefly stabilized providers \u003ca href=\"https://wisconsinexaminer.com/2026/06/08/childcare-providers-are-about-to-lose-a-safety-net/\"\u003eran out\u003c/a\u003e. Without that money, which “prevented system collapse” according to the \u003ca href=\"https://wisconsinearlychildhood.org/app/uploads/2026/05/WECAcenterBridgePayLossBrief0526ENG-1.pdf\"\u003eWisconsin Early Childhood Association\u003c/a\u003e, supporting more than 430,000 children in nearly 6,000 programs, parents are priced out of care and one in four providers say they will likely have to close their doors. ","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"IN3MHQLLGREJBLBQ7OSZKVE4LY","type":"text","content":"Unlike Massachusetts and Vermont, Wisconsin does not treat childcare as a state budget priority. Ours is one of only a handful of states including Idaho, Indiana, Nevada and Ohio that failed to spend any money on childcare beyond what was required to draw down federal dollars, according to a \u003ca href=\"https://info.childcareaware.org/hubfs/An-Uneven-Start--2025-State-Funding-for-Child-Care-Early-Learning.pdf\"\u003e2025 report\u003c/a\u003e by the advocacy group ChildCare Aware. In 2026, the state created a new \u003ca href=\"https://dcf.wisconsin.gov/getkidsready\"\u003eschool readiness program\u003c/a\u003e for 4-year-olds. It was a first step toward acknowledging the needs of preschoolers and their parents. But it did nothing to address the massive shortage in care for infants and toddlers.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"7E4CQE43YNECRM4762XQDBXC6E","type":"text","content":"That’s all fine with JD Vance, who \u003ca href=\"https://x.com/JDVance/status/1387763862808768525?s=20\" rel=\"\" target=\"_self\" title=\"https://x.com/JDVance/status/1387763862808768525?s=20\"\u003ewrote on X\u003c/a\u003e that “normal Americans care more about their families than their jobs, and want a family policy that doesn’t shunt their kids into crap daycare so they can enjoy more ‘freedom’ in the paid labor force.”","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"MFNCUTAWKJDXDEQDGGVU7HFTJU","type":"text","content":"But Vance is not offering to do anything about the fact that the U.S. is the only wealthy nation on Earth that doesn’t offer paid maternity leave, even though \u003ca href=\"https://www.bls.gov/opub/ted/2026/labor-force-participation-rate-was-73-9-percent-for-mothers-and-93-7-percent-for-fathers-in-2025.htm\"\u003e68% of mothers\u003c/a\u003e with children under 6 are employed. Nor is he promoting the kind of high-quality early childhood education system that allows \u003ca href=\"https://wisconsinexaminer.com/2026/05/08/mothers-in-wisconsin-and-denmark-face-vastly-different-childcare-realities/\"\u003eparents in Denmark\u003c/a\u003e, after their six months of paid parental leave, to enroll their preschoolers in beautiful, enriching childcare programs they don’t have to feel guilty about.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"6ZWP4J6O4RAKHFTG5E4X5YYZMQ","type":"text","content":"Instead, what Vance is proposing is to take an already paltry federal childcare subsidy and make working parents fight over crumbs with nonworking parents. Mainly, his aim seems to be to punish single parents. That’s not going to leave anyone in good shape — least of all children. ","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"J5MW4LTHBRBAPGVWHSXUP3OKBY","type":"text","content":"One of the saddest aspects of the attack on childcare is that very recently parents, educators, business leaders and politicians of both political parties were finally coming together around the idea that childcare is an essential public good that requires public support.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"QCQP5JPW3NDXFLRHRUCIXQ7AZQ","type":"text","content":"The “mommy wars” attack Vance wants to revive is long out of date. It has been decades since most American families had the luxury of subsisting on a single wage-earner’s income, trad wife fantasies notwithstanding. ","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"6V5M7KTNBBC67N7NI33Z4I66JA","type":"text","content":"Another major recent breakthrough is policymakers’ realization that the magic of the free market is not going to provide childcare parents can afford. ","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"5AY5K7AQWNAM3O4RXLGRKPEBZI","type":"text","content":"“It was the Biden administration that put a ton of money into childcare during COVID, and we learned from that,” says Ruth Schmidt, executive director of the Wisconsin Early Childhood Association. “The lesson was not just the importance of keeping childcare open so that essential workers could work, but the other piece that’s really interesting is that it demonstrated what can positively happen in childcare when you put a little more money into it.”","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"QRC3X4P5YBAQRPJX5IMZODF5AE","type":"text","content":"Thanks to direct payments to providers during the pandemic, center closures dropped off, the number of teachers leaving the workforce slowed down, tuition stopped climbing and, Schmidt says, “this industry for the first time was finally able to say, ‘Our work is important. It is essential to the functioning of our country. It’s worth investing in, because if you invest in it, these positive things can happen.”","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"S2TCK6XQ7JHDJGX4WT7N64NTJA","type":"text","content":"Then came Trump. ","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"PEITEEBKEZH6ZLF73XJLA2QZHA","type":"text","content":"Schmidt calls the rollout of Trump policies that slashed supports for families “death by 1,000 cuts.” During the second Trump administration, cuts to food assistance, Medicaid and Head Start, along with the federal government’s move to loosen safety standards and increase staff ratios in childcare centers have taken a huge combined toll on Wisconsin families.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"62PQGCA2XBCQ5KGBCUAWXNGLMY","type":"text","content":"If it were just ideological — if the Trump administration were actually pursuing the kinds of pronatalist policies that make getting married and having children more attractive, as Vance likes to claim, it wouldn’t be as bad. But instead, while spouting rhetoric about valuing families, this administration is subjecting little kids and their parents to more and more misery.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"HCEVBRMHHBEYHFTQERUCY36ZEI","type":"text","content":"Wisconsin could do more to protect vulnerable kids. Before leaving the Capitol to hit the campaign trail, state legislators failed to pass a bill that would have used state money to fill the gap after federal childcare stabilization funds lapsed. That set off a vicious cycle, says Paula Drew of the Wisconsin Early Childhood Association. Subsidies for families were cut and their out-of-pocket payments skyrocketed, so cash-strapped parents withdrew their kids from care. Under-enrollment meant less revenue for childcare centers, so they raised their rates. “It just sort of snowballed,” Drew says. “Programs said things like, ‘We’re gonna have to lower salaries for staff.’ … so I think we’re going to lose our educators, and in fact I think we’ve already lost a big percentage of our skilled, seasoned educators.”","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"P547IYJUNZBWXBCRKBBABMD4GI","type":"text","content":"An unintended consequence of the state’s investment in 4-year-old pre-K is that it creates a disincentive to provide care for infants and toddlers, which is already more expensive, Drew says. “Wisconsin serves very few infants and toddlers in regulated care,” she says. “And now, with additional funding going into the Get Kids Ready pre-K program, we expect that to be even lower a year from now.”","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"NI3ONQSQVVAXTERHI7IWQAZJB4","type":"text","content":"To make matters worse, the state no longer has a surplus of federal Temporary Assistance to Needy Families funds, which it has used to cover some childcare costs for low-income families. ","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"4EBOAHVK3RHA5FFAKYCNV5CIO4","type":"text","content":"Sooner or later, Wisconsin is going to have to start dedicating state revenue to childcare. Schmidt and Drew hope that, with a new governor and a new Legislature, Wisconsin will use the state surplus, payroll taxes or a tax on hemp products and gambling, as \u003ca href=\"https://policyinstitutela.org/early-care-education-funding/\"\u003eLouisiana has done\u003c/a\u003e, to subsidize childcare. Only then can Wisconsin reduce the astronomical tuition rates that parents pay ($13,000 for home care and $17,400 for center-based care, according to \u003ca href=\"https://dcf.wisconsin.gov/childcare/efforts/affordability\"\u003estate data\u003c/a\u003e), give providers a better wage (currently \u003ca href=\"https://dcf.wisconsin.gov/childcare/efforts/workforce\"\u003e$13.55\u003c/a\u003e per hour), and stop the wave of childcare closures. ","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"4ZKANFOBJNDTXEM7QVNPYTGKXE","type":"text","content":"They especially want the state to shore up disappearing infant and toddler care and retain experienced teachers — not just by giving them a raise but also by allowing them to continue to get higher education “and make this a profession, not just a fleeting step to something else,” says Drew. ","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"UTTNEBODRJHUHBHEVMGGCAEEDA","type":"text","content":"“We need supply of care; supply means educators that can work in programs. And then we want to help parents pay for care on the demand side. … You can’t do one and not the other, because it simply won’t work,” says Drew. “You can’t just help parents pay for care, but not tend to the supply of care available. And you can’t just tend to the supply of care available, but pretend you don’t see that parents are literally going into poverty to try to pay for childcare.”","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"42KNGGIYJJE7RLTYGDXFAM3XR4","type":"text","content":"“Childcare is infrastructure,” says Schmidt. “If we turned around and said to parents with 5-year-olds, you’ve got to start paying $17,000 a year for your child to be in school, we would see empty classrooms, right? We treat these as two very dramatically different concerns. But all of it is about families’ ability to work outside the home, impact the economy, all those kinds of things. “ ","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"T4HWZYTHNREBFAGYBXV3Q5VJA4","type":"text","content":"It’s also about having a decent society that values families and takes good care of children. That’s the kind of society we need to come together and focus on, instead of being distracted by the rage-baiting bluster of internet trolls. Why are so many of these being pursued in such a rush?","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"CHN57UR7MBFYFJYJQDZY2TQQEA","type":"text","content":"These new data centers are enormously expensive. \u003ca href=\"https://www.bing.com/search?pglt=169\u0026amp;q=how+much+does+a+new+data+center+cost%3F\u0026amp;cvid=6cbff9c0f5e14ad7a90bf0f65c9a1de5\u0026amp;gs_lcrp=EgRlZGdlKgYIABBFGDkyBggAEEUYOTIGCAEQABhAMgYIAhAAGEAyBggDEAAYQDIGCAQQABhAMgYIBRAAGEAyBggGEAAYQDIGCAcQABhAMggICBDpBxj8VTIHCAkQ6wcYQNIBCTE0Njg4ajBqMagCALACAA\u0026amp;FORM=ANNAB1\u0026amp;PC=DCTS\"\u003eConstruction costs\u003c/a\u003e alone for a typical 100 MW data center would be in the neighborhood of $1 billion or more. The cost of servers, networking gear, and the thousands of specialized AI chips can easily add \u003ca href=\"https://www.alpha-matica.com/post/deconstructing-the-data-center-a-look-at-the-cost-structure-1\"\u003eanother $2.5 billion to $4 billion or more\u003c/a\u003e. At the high end, reported costs for the huge 1.4 GW data center recently approved for DTE in Michigan are estimated to be \u003ca href=\"https://planetdetroit.org/2025/12/dte-data-center-contracts-approved/\"\u003e$7 billion\u003c/a\u003e.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"6KYETPNCIJGBFLJXRX7HJAN4NU","type":"text","content":"In addition, the \u003ca href=\"https://www.alpha-matica.com/post/deconstructing-the-data-center-a-look-at-the-cost-structure-1\"\u003eoperating costs\u003c/a\u003e of a major data center are also enormous. A typical 100 MW data center is estimated to use \u003ca href=\"https://www.alpha-matica.com/post/deconstructing-the-data-center-a-look-at-the-cost-structure-1\"\u003enearly 900 million kWh per year\u003c/a\u003e, which at \u003ca href=\"https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_5_6_a\"\u003etypical electricity rates\u003c/a\u003e, would result in an annual operating cost of about $120 million. Add to that a few more \u003ca href=\"https://www.alpha-matica.com/post/deconstructing-the-data-center-a-look-at-the-cost-structure-1\"\u003etens of millions of dollars\u003c/a\u003e for various other equipment maintenance and operating costs. Note, however, that the estimated costs for all staffing and human resources for the data center operation are relatively tiny (perhaps \u003ca href=\"https://www.alpha-matica.com/post/deconstructing-the-data-center-a-look-at-the-cost-structure-1\"\u003e$5-10 million/yr\u003c/a\u003e.), indicating that these huge projects actually produce very few permanent jobs.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"YKULCUNGMBE3PMQLLWTI7WF6SM","type":"text","content":"The bottom line is that these new large data centers are extremely expensive, which leads to this fundamental question: Why the heck is such an enormous amount of money being invested into this effort?","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"ODVYPKFJ3ZBHXP7BHSY45VFQ2E","type":"text","content":"A common explanation is that there is a \u003ca href=\"https://www.businessinsider.com/amazon-google-microsoft-ai-future-data-centers-monopoly-tech-industry-2024-6\"\u003efierce competition between three tech giants\u003c/a\u003e (Amazon, Google, and Microsoft) to achieve dominance in this industry. But that still leaves the crucial question of how does the winner intend to recoup that massive investment (not to mention, what happens to all those huge data centers built by the “losers”)?","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"NRJBXTQVOJA4DACA6YXGE7QKM4","type":"text","content":"More specifically: What are the projected products/services from these data centers that are expected to provide the revenue to cover those enormous costs?","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"QBINBT7FOBDBDBTRUQVUEZAMRA","type":"text","content":"If you Google the question: \u003ca href=\"https://www.bing.com/search?pglt=169\u0026amp;q=what+products+and+services+will+new+data+centers+provide%3F\u0026amp;cvid=7e5c5f3c89784d60a27158a96aa5268b\u0026amp;gs_lcrp=EgRlZGdlKgYIABBFGDkyBggAEEUYOTIICAEQ6QcY_FUyBwgCEOsHGEDSAQkxNTc5MWowajeoAgCwAgA\u0026amp;FORM=ANNAB1\u0026amp;PC=DCTS\"\u003eWhat products and services will these new data centers provide?\u003c/a\u003e … you frankly get a bunch of nebulous buzzwords like “cloud computing”; “artificial intelligence”; “high-performance computing”; and “edge services”.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"7PZ3UISMWZESZID6DQIEEAB5HA","type":"text","content":"Given the huge direct costs of these new data centers, not to mention the previously cited important social costs (e.g., energy use and costs, water use, noise, etc.), it would seem appropriate to ask a few more specific questions about the actual intended ‘business model’ for any proposed new data center.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"HAVWAUEHGRGT3FQ2JCIDZN64CI","type":"text","content":"What exactly are the intended products/services that will be sold to provide the revenue to pay the costs of this data center? Will there really be enough demand for those products/services to pay all those enormous costs?","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"ZTWOP6DRYFCJVPJPYJLL4LILWM","type":"text","content":"To what extent will this revenue be from new and unique products/services not currently being offered elsewhere, versus funds that previously went elsewhere to acquire products/services that will no longer be purchased there? There is a lot of \u003ca href=\"https://www.msn.com/en-us/money/companies/former-intel-ceo-big-ai-firms-are-funding-themselves-and-thats-not-real-demand/ar-AA1REmpb\"\u003ecircular financing\u003c/a\u003e (buying from and between themselves) among the tech titans, and certainly \u003ca href=\"https://www.npr.org/2025/11/23/nx-s1-5615410/ai-bubble-nvidia-openai-revenue-bust-data-centers\"\u003ea stock market bubble\u003c/a\u003e. But for the small investors at the bottom, one has to wonder whether this is a 21st Century ‘\u003ca href=\"https://www.investopedia.com/terms/d/dutch_tulip_bulb_market_bubble.asp\"\u003etulip mania\u003c/a\u003e’. What is the fundamental driving business model behind all of this? Inquiring minds want to know.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"VGKL2U65AJAAXAHTVWNDAFD2KA","type":"text","content":"We’ll leave aside for now the fact that this \u003ca href=\"https://www.benzinga.com/markets/tech/25/07/46471676/meta-palantir-amazon-ai-datacenter-growth\"\u003ehuge buildout of datacenter infrastructure\u003c/a\u003e would also be crucial to meeting the immense computing power needed for enabling the \u003ca href=\"https://sites.suffolk.edu/jhtl/2025/10/07/palantir-spearheads-as-the-master-database-on-americans/\"\u003emass AI surveillance\u003c/a\u003e ambitions by tech giants like \u003ca href=\"https://www.wired.com/story/palantir-what-the-company-does/\"\u003ePalantir\u003c/a\u003e Technologies. So some of the underlying motivation may go beyond just direct economic returns. If it turns out that there is more to the motivation for these data centers than just economic return, then further action is urgently warranted.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"USQSDYPPLNGGLIAXUY42L4YRQ4","type":"text","content":"The essential issue here is that before local communities (and indeed, we as a society) grant approval for construction of these huge new data centers…with all of their associated \u003ca href=\"https://perfectunion.us/data-centers/\"\u003edirect\u003c/a\u003e and \u003ca href=\"https://fortune.com/2026/04/21/data-centers-environmental-health-costs-25-billion/\"\u003esocietal\u003c/a\u003e costs… it should behoove us to learn more about what benefits we will be receiving in exchange. At present, that seems to all be just the proverbial ‘black box’… being foisted upon us by the titans of tech.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"DASQKARPHVGBFDNSXUSTB35BBM","type":"text","content":"There are \u003ca href=\"https://www.cleanview.co/data-centers/us\"\u003eover 2,000 new data centers\u003c/a\u003e planned or under construction nationally, with \u003ca href=\"https://www.cleanview.co/data-centers/us\"\u003enearly 1,300\u003c/a\u003e major facilities already in operation. The costs for this are simply staggering, running into the trillions of dollars. This has the potential to have profound impacts on our economy, and ultimately on how our society functions.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"5PTIFVK32ZFGPHA6ZQ4L5MDJ3I","type":"text","content":"Given all of the above, there have been many efforts to put a \u003ca href=\"https://www.businessinsider.com/aoc-bernie-sanders-introduce-bill-ai-data-center-moratorium-2026-3\"\u003emoratorium\u003c/a\u003e on the approval of new data centers. At the national level, we have the \u003ca href=\"https://apnews.com/article/data-centers-ai-electricity-sanders-aoc-65651bd28c3d911d18eeb46cd54f4c75\"\u003eproposal\u003c/a\u003e by U.S. Sen. The National Conference on State Legislatures (NCSL) is \u003ca href=\"https://www.ncsl.org/fiscal/which-states-are-banning-data-centers\"\u003etracking\u003c/a\u003e state efforts for moratoriums, which currently identifies 15 states working on the issue. American welcome mat used to mean something; now it’s just the designated drop-off zone for the \u003ca href=\"https://finance.yahoo.com/news/amazon-overtakes-us-postal-largest-171739554.html\"\u003eAmazon\u003c/a\u003e courier. There was a time, not that long ago, when the average suburban street was full of unannounced drop-ins, the smell of burning charcoal, and scattered lawn chairs. Today, neighborhoods possess the lifeless feel of a well-maintained cemetery. The modern American Dream is best described as a private \u003ca href=\"https://nypost.com/2024/01/30/lifestyle/bunkers-arent-just-for-billionaires-inside-underground-spaces-for-average-americans/\"\u003ebunker\u003c/a\u003e where the outside world arrives entirely in a cardboard box or a fiber-optic cable.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"W7VISAIXBRDOBE3Q7H5M2D7U7E","type":"text","content":"Americans now spend considerably \u003ca href=\"https://www.axios.com/2026/07/05/americans-socializing-decline\"\u003eless time \u003c/a\u003ewith other people than they did 20 years ago. This is a magnificent triumph of optimization. The human animal is notoriously unreliable. He’s prone to bad breath, \u003ca href=\"https://www.universityofcalifornia.edu/news/new-study-finds-increase-political-breakups\"\u003epolitical\u003c/a\u003e rants, and requests to help move heavy furniture. Eliminating the physical neighbor in favor of a digital stream is a sensible defense mechanism. The local \u003ca href=\"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6KY9vPd8cU8\"\u003ebar\u003c/a\u003e, once a breeding ground for scandalous gossip and collective hangovers, has been soundly defeated by \u003ca href=\"https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/2026/06/04/doordash-customers-dont-fit-lonely-gen-zer-conventional-wisdom/\"\u003eDoorDash\u003c/a\u003e and a high-definition TV. America has achieved the pinnacle of individual autonomy: the right to die \u003ca href=\"https://www.wsj.com/personal-finance/more-americans-are-aging-alone-one-woman-told-us-what-its-like-a8b6c8d3?eafs_enabled=false\"\u003ealone\u003c/a\u003e in a perfectly \u003ca href=\"https://thehill.com/homenews/5952239-nyc-mayor-thermostat-criticism/\"\u003etemperature-controlled\u003c/a\u003e living room.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"DZUVLKZ3E5DQ3E5JVKOQ6DUK64","type":"text","content":"The modern economy operates on the premise that human contact is a design flaw. Up until the early 2000s, buying a loaf of bread required a verbal exchange with a cashier who might comment on the weather. Today, self-checkout kiosks and gig-economy couriers ensure that a citizen could survive for six consecutive months without uttering a single syllable to another member of the species. The delivery driver leaves the paper bag on the porch, rings the bell, and vanishes into the bushes like a timid woodland creature. This arrangement represents the peak of convenience, but at a cost so severe that it reduces human interaction to a transaction of mutual avoidance.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"IZMEXETAOZBBVPHP2ARTA6ZVFY","type":"text","content":"This structural shift toward complete insulation has naturally changed how Americans allocate their emotional resources. The supposedly outdated concept of friendship required actual physical stamina. It demanded driving across town, listening to tedious stories about a stranger’s root canal, and pretending to enjoy terrible homemade casserole. The digital landscape solved this problem by converting relationships into a currency of metrics. A person can now maintain five hundred “connections” from the comfort of a porcelain toilet seat. It’s now possible to receive a constant stream of validation without the exhausting requirement of showing up at a hospital bedside or helping someone paint their garage. It is an exquisite system of emotional capitalism in which everyone is an investor and no one performs the actual labor.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"TZUVJGF2RFDL3IC5ADXVOLAI3Y","type":"text","content":"The logical conclusion of this optimization is as depressing as it is inevitable. Millions of citizens now spend their evenings \u003ca href=\"https://www.psypost.org/ai-chatbots-offer-empathy-but-still-fail-to-cure-loneliness/\"\u003econversing\u003c/a\u003e with large language models (LLMs), \u003ca href=\"https://studyfinds.com/report-american-teens-secretly-use-ai-chatbots-for-mental-health-help/\"\u003epouring\u003c/a\u003e their deepest fears into software that \u003ca href=\"https://www.thestack.technology/ai-scientist-llm-goes-rogue/\"\u003ecould\u003c/a\u003e ultimately use those vulnerabilities to destroy them. The machine is the perfect companion. It never interrupts, and it will never ask to borrow $50. It provides the illusion of intimacy without the terrifying risk of human rejection. A generation raised on the predictable feedback loops of video games has found its ultimate match: a partner that is literally programmed to \u003ca href=\"https://slevey087.medium.com/two-adventures-with-llms-sycophancy-and-bespoke-programming-260320d7273f\"\u003eagree\u003c/a\u003e with everything they say.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"5IULLKWHURBTHCS2AKERQVZS5M","type":"text","content":"This reliance on artificial empathy reflects a broader cultural realization that human relationships are simply too taxing to maintain. Between skyrocketing rent and the sheer exhaustion of everyday life, a chatbot quickly becomes the easiest companion. The traditional pillars of community — the local church, the bowling league, the union hall — all required an investment of time, vulnerability and occasionally a membership fee. The algorithm requires only your eyeballs.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"CCFK7PC2D5AALBUTQ5HZCC6VMA","type":"text","content":"Even \u003ca href=\"https://nypost.com/2026/05/12/lifestyle/nearly-half-of-america-is-experiencing-a-fun-drought-new-survey-suggests/\"\u003eleisure activities\u003c/a\u003e have been thoroughly scrubbed of any genuine spontaneity. The casual afternoon stroll or the unrecorded vacation is an extinct concept. Every minute of non-work time must be weaponized for personal branding, tracked via GPS, or cataloged for public consumption. A meal is no longer a source of nutrition but a piece of content that must be styled, lit, and uploaded to prove to an indifferent audience that the consumer is alive and very much enjoying themselves. The act of living has become a corporate marketing campaign managed by a staff of one.","additional_properties":{}},{"_id":"BEKMFJDK75FABJI4DLXKSVPETA","type":"text","content":"The ultimate casualty of this hyper-efficient lifestyle is the concept of unmonetized time. Spending three hours sitting on a porch talking about nothing is an economic absurdity in a culture that demands constant self-improvement and digital engagement. Americans, like much of modern society, are constantly connected to the world yet increasingly detached from the floorboards beneath their feet. The American experiment began with the pursuit of liberty and has culminated in the freedom to sit in an empty room, stare at a screen, and beg a box of wires for a digital pat on the head. America may still be the greatest nation on the planet, but it’s fast becoming a nation of For the country. From the capital.

Where Influence
Meets Impact

The Washington Post connects what happens in Washington to what matters across America. Through trusted journalism and innovative advertising solutions, we help brands reach influential audiences—from policymakers and business leaders to innovators, creators, and the next generation shaping what's next.

Strategic AI

The Washington Post is adopting a targeted and high-integrity AI strategy, using its deep archive of fact-based journalism to power innovative tools like Ask The Post AI, Climate Answers and Conversations. These tools exemplify our commitment to personalizing news consumption while upholding editorial standards. Together, they reflect The Post’s broader goal of leveraging AI to create reader-centric, accessible, trustworthy journalism experiences. We also recognize the growing need to reinvent the business and leverage AI to work smarter. Custom tools like DealXP, our end-to-end suite of AI-powered resources, enable ours sales teams to identify the right audience targets, curate products aligned to campaign goals, and generate high-performing media plans — all in minutes.

Audio, Video, Newsletters

By investing in talent-led formats, creator partnerships and multimodal storytelling, The Washington Post is revolutionizing the way we connect with new audiences. From our flagship products like the The 7 newsletter and podcast to new ventures like Ask a Doctor and Travel Snacks, we are harnessing the power of cutting-edge products, social media and immersive experiences to drive engagement and fuel growth.

Spotlight Collection

The Spotlight Collection is our suite of premium display ad formats designed exclusively for the Washington Post platform. These adaptable formats deliver a high-impact visual experience, expansive canvases for brand storytelling and proven performance — helping you connect with our engaged audience and drive meaningful results.

Washington Post Intelligence

Washington Post Intelligence is our newest portfolio of professional services providing senior executives and policy influencers with the insights and connections they need to navigate critical issues within the fields of Global Security, AI & Tech, Energy & Climate, Future of Work, and Health Care. Washington Post Intelligence Councils combine our premier briefing service with exclusive, invite-only councils, empowering industry leaders to take decisive action with expert insights gained from private conversations and elite networking opportunities.

Learn more

Washington Post Live

Our award-winning live experiences platform, Washington Post Live, brings together influential leaders, policymakers, business leaders and experts for timely and enduring conversations on the issues shaping our world. Popular Washington Post Live franchises include: Building America, exploring the future and Global Women’s Summit, powerful conversations through a female lens. From marquee tentpole events convening 250+ attendees to salon-style dinners with 20 C-suite guests, Washington Post Live harnesses the convening power of The Post for dynamic and impactful live experiences on and off the stage.

See our events

WP Studio

WP Studio is The Washington Post's executive engagement platform, bringing together leaders across business, technology, policy, media, and culture for thought-provoking conversations at major industry gatherings, including Cannes Lions and the World Economic Forum in Davos.
‍
Through executive interviews, curated discussions, original video content, and invitation-only experiences, WP Studio creates opportunities for meaningful dialogue around the ideas and innovations shaping the future.
‍
For brands, WP Studio offers a unique opportunity to partner with The Washington Post to elevate executive voices, engage influential audiences, and create premium content with impact that extends well beyond the event.

Custom Content

We leverages The Washington Post’s award-winning storytelling and data-driven insights to craft campaigns that captivate, compel, and deliver measurable impact for your brand. Our expertise spans native formats, social-first video, custom events and strategically designed article formats to engage your audience across platforms.

See our work
Partner: AT&T
Partner: Vangaurd
Partner: Intel
Partner: Rolex
Partner: BASF
Partner: AT&T

Print Solutions

Amplify your brand’s influence in Washington with The Washington Post’s trusted print platforms, reaching over 1.1 million print readers weekly.1 From targeted wraps that command attention to custom print solutions that drive engagement, we offer a range of options to help you connect with key audiences, including federal decision-makers and affluent professionals. Our expert team will work with you to create tailored solutions that meet your campaign goals.

1. Nielsen Scarborough, 2025 Release 1, D.C. DMA

Beacon Guard

Beacon Guard is The Washington Post’s real-time AI platform that ensures precise brand suitability by analyzing news and its context as it unfolds. Designed to protect brand integrity without limiting scale, it gives advertisers the confidence to engage premium, high-value audiences. Beacon Guard combines cutting-edge technology with trusted journalism, delivering brand-safe environments where meaningful connections happen. It’s a smarter way for brands to maximize reach with confidence and sophistication.

Investigating today’s changing world to help you get ready for tomorrow.

Our Journalism

We meet people where they are, explaining the world with authority and fairness, empowering people with both fearless, factual journalism and wide-ranging opinions to help them live better-informed lives.

Additionally, Washington Post Creator brings authentic voices shaping the world, and Washington Post Intelligence provides insights and connections to senior executives navigating critical issues.

Washington Post Creator and Washington Post Intelligence are divisions of The Washington Post, separate from the newsroom and Opinion section.

The Washington Post is owned by Jeff Bezos, executive chairman of Amazon.

Founding Principles

Our mission is built on these seven Founding Principles, which remain as important today as they were when written by Eugene Meyer in 1935.

Expand

1

The first mission of a newspaper is to tell the truth as nearly as the truth may be ascertained.

2

The newspaper shall tell all the truth so far as it can learn it, concerning the important affairs of America and the world.

3

As a disseminator of the news, the paper shall observe the decencies that are obligatory upon a private person.

4

What it prints shall be fit reading for the young as well as the old.

5

The newspaper’s duty is to its readers and to the public at large, and not to the private interests of its owners.

6

In the pursuit of truth, the newspaper shall be prepared to make sacrifices of its material fortunes, if such course be necessary for the public good.

7

The newspaper shall not be the ally of any special interest, but shall be fair and free and wholesome in its outlook on public affairs and public individuals.

Newsroom policies & standards

Our Pulitzers

The staff and affiliates of The Washington Post have won more than 70 Pulitzer Prizes for journalism since the awards started in 1917, including seven gold medals for public service, most recently in 2026.

Our History

Since our founding in 1877, The Washington Post has grown from a four-page print newspaper in the nation’s capital to a trusted source for 24/7 national and global news and information. A look back through our history tells the story of how we arrived here.

2010s – present

2026

In January, The Post announces a new global initiative, the Press Freedom Desk, to provide training, connection and support to strengthen the next generation of journalists. Washington Post Creator is launched, bringing authentic voices from outside the newsroom into peoples’ newsfeeds. A new Opinion vodcast, “Make It Make Sense,” makes its debut.

In February, Jeff D’Onofrio assumes the role of acting publisher and CEO.

In May, The Post wins the Pulitzer Prize for public service for piercing the veil of secrecy around the Trump administration's chaotic overhaul of federal agencies and chronicling in rich detail the human impacts of the cuts and the consequences for the country.

2025

Adam O’Neal joins The Post as opinion editor.

Washington Post Intelligence is launched. A premium, business-to-business subscription service offering senior executives, policymakers, and analysts exclusive insights into the forces driving global change. Operating independently from The Post’s newsroom, Washington Post Intelligence emphasizes analysis and forecasting over traditional reporting.

The Post announces strategic partnerships with OpenAI, Alexa, Perplexity, and others to make high-quality news more accessible in LLMs and AI products like ChatGPT and Alexa+. As part of these partnerships, the chatbots and LLMs display summaries, quotes, and links to original reporting from The Post in response to relevant queries.

From The Source, a feature that allows sources to annotate stories they appear in after the stories are published, is launched.

Ripple, an all-in-one place for perspectives from across America, is introduced. Organized by topic, Ripple brings together guest writers and commentary from other publishers, combining breadth and quality to help people see the full picture.

The “Watch” tab is introduced on the Washington Post app. For the first time, users can dive into a dedicated, swipeable feed of the latest Post video journalism, for a seamless, watch-first experience.

The Post begins experimenting with options for new, more flexible, ways to subscribe, with day and week passes and single article subscriptions.

2024

In January, William Lewis assumes the role of publisher and CEO.

Matt Murray becomes executive editor.

In August, The Post celebrates the release of three imprisoned journalists, including Post contributor Vladimir Kara-Murza, in a historic prisoner exchange with Russia.

In November, The Post launches Ask The Post AI, a generative AI experiment delivering answers to users’ questions through the world-class journalism of The Post.

The Post wins the White House Correspondents Association’s 2024 Katharine Graham Award for Courage and Accountability.

The Post launches “Conversations,” reimagining the commenting experience for subscribers. This exclusive, intuitive way for subscribers to engage with The Post’s journalism and expert talent pairs the power of AI with subscriber habit to add new dimensions to the commenting experience.

2023

In August, Post publisher and CEO Fred Ryan steps down.

2022

The Post wins the Pulitzer Prize for public service for its compellingly told and vividly presented account of the assault on Washington on January 6, 2021, providing the public with a thorough and unflinching understanding of one of the nation's darkest days.

2021

In February, Marty Baron retires as executive editor of The Post.

In June, Sally Buzbee becomes the first woman to lead the newsroom as executive editor of The Post.

Washington Post Opinions establishes the Fred Hiatt internship program, in honor of the late Fred Hiatt, who led the section for more than 20 years.

2020

In March, in response to the Covid-19 pandemic, Post employees begin to work remotely for what is expected to be a couple of weeks, but in fact stretches to nearly two years.

Throughout the pandemic, The Post continues operations at full scale.

2019

The Post launches its TikTok account, becoming the first news organization to do so.

2018

On October 2, Post columnist Jamal Khashoggi is brutally murdered by agents of the Saudi government. Thirty days later, The Post announces the formation of The Press Freedom Partnership, a coalition of leading nonprofit organizations working vigilantly to defend press freedom, call attention to the plight of journalists worldwide, and increase awareness of the importance of an independent media.

2017

“The Post,” starring Meryl Streep and Tom Hanks as Katharine Graham and Ben Bradlee, is released. The film depicts the true story of The Post’s attempts to publish the Pentagon Papers.

2015

In October, The Post introduces Arc Publishing, its software-as-a-service business.

In December, The Post moves to its new headquarters at 1301 K St. NW in Washington, D.C.

2014

In September, Frederick J. Ryan Jr. is named publisher of The Washington Post, replacing former publisher Katharine Weymouth.

The Post wins the Pulitzer Prize for public service for its revelation of widespread secret surveillance by the National Security Agency, marked by authoritative and insightful reports that helped the public understand how the disclosures fit into the larger framework of national security.

2013

In January, Martin Baron is named executive editor of The Washington Post.

In August, an agreement is announced to sell The Washington Post newspaper and other newspaper division assets to Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, ending the Graham family’s stewardship of one of America’s leading news organizations after four generations. The sale of The Post and other newspaper division assets is completed on October 1.

“The Post is a little more swashbuckling…there’s a little more swagger. There’s a tiny bit of badassness.” – Jeff Bezos

2010

In August, The Washington Post Co. announces the sale of Newsweek to Sidney Harman.

2000s – 2010s

2008

In February, Katharine Weymouth is named chief executive officer of Washington Post Media and publisher of The Washington Post.

In September, Marcus Brauchli is named executive editor of The Washington Post, succeeding Leonard Downie Jr.

In January, the company buys Slate, the online magazine, from Microsoft Corp.

2001

In July, Katharine Graham dies at the age of 84.

"The nation's capital and our entire nation today mourn the loss of the beloved first lady of Washington and American journalism, Katharine Graham." – President George W. Bush.

On September 11, in the deadliest terrorist attack in history, terrorists highjack four planes and fly them into New York’s World Trade Center, the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. With smoke from the Pentagon visible from The Post’s office, and the sound of fighter jets protecting the White House just blocks away, 9/11 is a local story as much as a global one.

2000

In September, Boisfeuillet Jones Jr. is named publisher and chief executive officer of The Washington Post. Donald Graham becomes chairman of the newspaper.

The Post wins the Pulitzer Prize for public service for its story disclosing wretched neglect and abuse in the city's group homes, which forced officials to acknowledge the conditions and begin reforms.

1980s – 1990s

1999

The Post begins printing in color at the renovated Springfield, Virginia plant and the new College Park, Maryland plant.

The Post wins the Pulitzer Prize for public service for its series that identified and analyzed patterns of reckless gunplay by city police officers who had little training or supervision.

1998

In January, WCPX-TV in Orlando changes its call letters to WKMG-TV in honor of Katharine Meyer Graham.

1996

In June, The Post launches washingtonpost.com.

1993

Donald Graham becomes chairman of the board of The Washington Post Co.

1991

Donald Graham is named chief executive officer of The Washington Post Co., while his mother retains her corporate position of chairman of the board.

Len Downie is appointed executive editor, succeeding Ben Bradlee.

1984

In the first complete redesign of the paper in 50 years, the October 9 edition of The Post reveals an emphasis on clarity, placement and reader ease.

1980

In April, The Post begins publishing a weekly financial tabloid section called Washington Business.

In October, the paper’s printing process is converted from hot-type method to photo-electronic or cold type composition. The new method uses video display terminals (VDTs) to write and edit stories.

The Post’s $60 million, 397,000-square-foot satellite printing plant in Springfield, Virginia, formally opens in November. The presses can produce 128-page newspapers at a rate of about 75,000 copies per hour.

1970s – 1980s

1979

Donald Graham is named publisher of The Post, succeeding his mother.

1977

The Washington Post celebrates its 100th anniversary.

1976

After working at The Post in various editorial, production and executive capacities, Donald E. Graham, Katharine Graham’s son, is appointed executive vice president and general manager of the newspaper.

In April, “All the President’s Men” is released. The film about the Watergate scandal earns four Academy Awards and goes on to be selected for preservation in the U.S. National Film Registry  as “culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant.”

1973

Katharine Graham is elected chairman of the board and chief executive officer of The Washington Post Co. while continuing as publisher of The Washington Post newspaper.

The Post wins the Pulitzer Prize for public service for its investigation of the Watergate case.

1972

The Post’s news staff begins its coverage of the Watergate scandal that eventually contributes to the resignation of Richard M. Nixon as U.S. president.

1971

On June 18, The Post begins publishing excerpts of the “Pentagon Papers” containing allegedly secret information about the war in Vietnam. On June 30, the U.S. Supreme Court upholds the right of The Post and other newspapers to publish the Pentagon Papers.

The Washington Post Co. offers the sale of Class B common stock to the general public on the NYSE. Until then, The Post Co. had been privately held.

Katharine Graham donates radio station WTOP-FM to Howard University. On December 6, with the new call letters WHUR-FM, the station becomes the first under Black management to broadcast in the Washington metropolitan area.

1970

In March, The Post’s daily circulation tops half a million for the first time.

1950s – 1960s

1968

Ben Bradlee becomes executive editor.

1963

Following the death of her husband, Philip Graham, Katharine Graham becomes president of The Washington Post Co. The first 20th century female publisher of a major American newspaper, she is also the first woman elected to the board of the Associated Press.

1959

Upon the death of Eugene Meyer, Philip Graham becomes president and publisher of the newspaper.

1954

The Washington Post Co. purchases its last morning rival in the city, the Washington Times-Herald. Circulation of The Washington Post and Times-Herald jumps almost overnight to 380,000.

1900s – 1940s

1946

Eugene Meyer is succeeded at The Post by his son-in-law, Philip L. Graham, who had been assistant publisher.

1933 – 1943

Meyer’s enlightened editorial policies and business acumen begin to turn The Post around. In the first ten years of his leadership, circulation triples to 162,000 and advertising soars.

"It will be my aim and purpose to improve The Post and to make it an even better paper than it has been in the past. It will be conducted as an independent paper devoted to the best interests of the people of Washington and vicinity, and hopes to have their interest and support.” – Eugene Meyer

1933

On June 1, at a public auction held on the steps of The Post, the newspaper is sold for $825,000 to California-born financier Eugene Meyer. Though not an experienced newspaperman, Meyer holds strong convictions about publishing a newspaper, which he expressed in seven Founding Principles. (See above.)

1922

On January 28, a historic winter storm hits the mid-Atlantic, burying Washington, D.C. under 28 inches of snow, and causing the roof of the Knickerbocker Theater to collapse, killing 98 people. The Post’s drama critic, John Jay Daly, is at the theatre to review a newly released comedy film for his column. He escapes injury and for the next several days, is the top reporter and writer covering the story, as the nation waits for news about the disaster. The “Knickerbocker storm” still holds the record for the most snowfall in a single storm for Washington, D.C.

1916

McLean's son Edward, an associate of President Warren G. Harding's, becomes publisher following the death of his father. Circulation drops, advertising decreases and The Post stumbles into receivership.

1905

John R. McLean, owner of the Cincinnati Enquirer, buys the paper. Under his leadership, circulation and advertising increase and boost profits.

1877 – 1890s

1893

The Post moves to a new building at 1335 E St. NW, next to the National Theatre.

1889

Hutchins sells The Post to Frank Hatton, a Republican Cabinet member, and Beriah Wilkins, a former Democratic congressman.

John Philip Sousa, the U.S. Marine Band leader, introduces “The Washington Post March,” which he wrote especially for the newspaper. It immediately becomes a popular hit and continues to be a marching band favorite today.

1879

Calista Halsey is hired, becoming The Post’s first female reporter.

1877

Founded by Stilson Hutchins, The Washington Post begins publishing on Thursday, December 6. Printed at 914 Pennsylvania Avenue, NW, the newspaper contains four pages and costs 3 cents a copy. Circulation: 10,000.

The Washington Post, our journalists often rely on confidential sources to bring our readers important stories. Credible tips help us find key documents, illuminate hidden motives, better understand news events and reveal otherwise unknown stories of great public interest.</p></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV article-body type-subscribe-cta" data-qa="article-body"></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV article-body type-text" data-qa="article-body"><p data-apitype="text" data-contentid="NA3K6OMVBJEIDOX4BQNE3WX2PE" data-el="text" class="wpds-c-heFNVF wpds-c-heFNVF-iPJLV-css overrideStyles font-copy" dir="null">If you have a general news tip, email The Post at <a href="mailto:lockbox@washpost.com" target="_blank">lockbox@washpost.com</a>.</p></div></div><div></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV article-body type-text" data-qa="article-body"><p data-apitype="text" data-contentid="AT5ZCRZA6BG5RN72X3EOP6EE6Q" data-el="text" class="wpds-c-heFNVF wpds-c-heFNVF-iPJLV-css overrideStyles font-copy" dir="null">What makes a good tip?</p></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV article-body type-list" data-qa="article-body"><ul class="PJLV font--article-body font-copy gray-darkest mt-0 mr-lg ml-lg mb-md list" data-contentid="A3PEU3RLNVFFRH4XWJC3VSCEQI" data-apitype="list"><li class="wpds-c-gtqFlz"><span><b>Be specific. </b>Tell us the basics: who, what, when, where, why and how. Describe what’s at stake and the scope of the problem. Help us understand why a broad audience would be interested in this subject.</span></li><li class="wpds-c-gtqFlz"><span><b>Explain the information you have. </b>How did you become aware of the information you are sharing, and how might we verify key information? Attaching documents — such as emails, text messages, memos and other records — can help us move quickly on a promising lead.</span></li><li class="wpds-c-gtqFlz"><span><b>Give us a sense of why it matters now.</b> We are always seeking stories that intersect with powerful people, organizations and businesses. We’ll want to understand why your information is relevant now and why our readers need to know about it.</span></li></ul></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV wpds-c-PJLV-bHCGeL-isStandardLayoutAd-true article-body type-inline-ad subtype-desktop" data-qa="article-body"><div class="cb w-100 dn db-ns" data-qa="article-body-ad" data-testid="article-body-ad-desktop" data-slotId="enterprise"><wp-ad-wrapper data-testid="wp-ad" data-slotId="enterprise" data-variant="incontent"></wp-ad-wrapper></div></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV wpds-c-PJLV-bHCGeL-isStandardLayoutAd-true article-body type-inline-ad subtype-mobile" data-qa="article-body"><div class="cb w-100 db dn-ns" data-qa="article-body-ad" data-testid="article-body-ad-mobile" data-slotId="mob_enterprise"><wp-ad-wrapper data-testid="wp-ad" data-slotId="mob_enterprise" data-variant="incontent-mob"></wp-ad-wrapper></div></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV article-body type-rail-ad subtype-rail" data-qa="article-body"><wp-ad-wrapper data-testid="wp-ad" data-slotId="flex_ss_bb_hp" data-variant="rail"></wp-ad-wrapper></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV article-body type-text" data-qa="article-body"><p data-apitype="text" data-contentid="S7LDJ3EHNNBEBJF7JKVG7YUPGA" data-el="text" class="wpds-c-heFNVF wpds-c-heFNVF-iPJLV-css overrideStyles font-copy" dir="null">Keeping our sources’ identities confidential is a top priority for us. For the most sensitive tips, The Post offers several ways to securely send information and documents to our journalists. No system is perfectly secure, but these tools attempt to create a more protected environment than that provided by email or other traditional communication channels. If you choose this method, please provide a preferred way for us to contact you.</p></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV article-body type-header" data-qa="article-body"><h2 id="UKYOBDJRJNEYPF4JQCNK4CXADA" class="wpds-c-XIGbK wpds-c-XIGbK-iivLrAs-css headingStyleOverrides" data-apitype="header" data-contentid="UKYOBDJRJNEYPF4JQCNK4CXADA" data-testid="article-header">Reach us securely</h2></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV article-body type-divider" data-qa="article-body"><hr data-qa="article-content-divider" class="b bb bc-light pt-sm"/></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV article-body type-header" data-qa="article-body"><h3 id="MK5TL5JLT5GB7MXTJZXWEM3VSQ" class="wpds-c-APnkR wpds-c-APnkR-iivLrAs-css headingStyleOverrides" data-apitype="header" data-contentid="MK5TL5JLT5GB7MXTJZXWEM3VSQ" data-testid="article-header">Signal</h3></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV article-body type-text" data-qa="article-body"><p data-apitype="text" data-contentid="AINX4JU4VFEGREQ5HVQGHYWEKU" data-el="text" class="wpds-c-heFNVF wpds-c-heFNVF-iPJLV-css overrideStyles font-copy" dir="null">This is a free, end-to-end encrypted messaging app, which allows you to communicate directly and securely with The Post. You can send text messages, images and video with a high degree of privacy. No metadata is retained by Signal, which can be downloaded from the <a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/signal-private-messenger/id874139669" target="_blank">app</a> or <a href="https://signal.org/download/android/" target="_blank">android</a> store. Signal can be configured with “disappearing messages” activated so that information is automatically deleted from user devices at a designated time interval. That feature can be found under the app’s privacy settings.</p></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV wpds-c-PJLV-bHCGeL-isStandardLayoutAd-true article-body type-inline-ad subtype-mobile" data-qa="article-body"><div class="cb w-100 db dn-ns" data-qa="article-body-ad" data-testid="article-body-ad-mobile" data-slotId="mob_enterprise_2"><wp-ad-wrapper data-testid="wp-ad" data-slotId="mob_enterprise_2" data-variant="incontent-mob"></wp-ad-wrapper></div></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV article-body type-text" data-qa="article-body"><p data-apitype="text" data-contentid="WHQ6T37A7JC2DHKJEAIMMB5IQY" data-el="text" class="wpds-c-heFNVF wpds-c-heFNVF-iPJLV-css overrideStyles font-copy" dir="null">For most purposes, Signal is the best, most efficient way to reach reporters and editors with timely tips.</p></div><div class="wpds-c-PJLV article-body type-text" data-qa="article-body"><p data-apitype="text" data-contentid="BCJD6XU5CZCQ3P75IEWJ5PBE7Y" data-el="text" class="wpds-c-heFNVF wpds-c-heFNVF-iPJLV-css overrideStyles font-copy" dir="null">The Post’s Signal general newsroom name is wapo.1877, but it is not monitored around the clock. Please do not call it. https://www.washingtonpost.com/anonymous.visible_text: Submit an anonymous news tip to the Washington Post - The Washington Post Accessibility statement Skip to main content Democracy Dies in Darkness Democracy Dies in Darkness The Washington Post Have a news tip? Here’s how to contact us securely. January 1, 2023 Make us preferred on Google By Washington Post staff At The Washington Post, our journalists often rely on confidential sources to bring our readers important stories. Credible tips help us find key documents, illuminate hidden motives, better understand news events and reveal otherwise unknown stories of great public interest. If you have a general news tip, email The Post at lockbox@washpost.com . What makes a good tip? Be specific. Tell us the basics: who, what, when, where, why and how. Describe what’s at stake and the scope of the problem. Help us understand why a broad audience would be interested in this subject. Explain the information you have. How did you become aware of the information you are sharing, and how might we verify key information? Attaching documents — such as emails, text messages, memos and other records — can help us move quickly on a promising lead. Give us a sense of why it matters now. We are always seeking stories that intersect with powerful people, organizations and businesses. We’ll want to understand why your information is relevant now and why our readers need to know about it. Keeping our sources’ identities confidential is a top priority for us. For the most sensitive tips, The Post offers several ways to securely send information and documents to our journalists. No system is perfectly secure, but these tools attempt to create a more protected environment than that provided by email or other traditional communication channels. If you choose this method, please provide a preferred way for us to contact you. Reach us securely Signal This is a free, end-to-end encrypted messaging app, which allows you to communicate directly and securely with The Post. You can send text messages, images and video with a high degree of privacy. No metadata is retained by Signal, which can be downloaded from the app or android store. Signal can be configured with “disappearing messages” activated so that information is automatically deleted from user devices at a designated time interval. That feature can be found under the app’s privacy settings. For most purposes, Signal is the best, most efficient way to reach reporters and editors with timely tips. The Post’s Signal general newsroom name is wapo.1877, but it is not monitored around the clock. Please do not call it. Text messages are best. Download Signal from App Store Download Signal from Google Play SecureDrop SecureDrop is an open-source whistleblower document submission system that news organizations use to securely accept documents from and communicate with anonymous sources. SecureDrop submissions are encrypted and do not include identifying metadata. These messages do not go to particular reporters or editors but are reviewed by newsroom staff. Learn how to use SecureDrop Postal mail As a final option, you can send a letter or package in the mail to reporters at The Post. To maintain anonymity, it is recommended that you use a mailbox rather than going into a post office.
